quote_orig: καὶ οὕτω μὲν ὑπὸ ζῶντος ἐποιήθην, καὶ εἰς τὸ κοινὸν γραμματεῖον ἐνεγράφην Θράσυλλος Ἀπολλοδώρου, ποιησαμένου με ἐκείνου τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον, τῶν νόμων αὐτῷ δεδωκότων.
quote_en: Thus I was adopted by him in his lifetime and my name inscribed in the public register as Thrasyllus the son of Apollodorus, after he had adopted me in this manner, as the laws have given him the power to do.
licence_note: Forster (Loeb 1927) translation; no licence line on the page read. Greek text from the same Perseids edition (Forster ed.).
from_: Thus I was adopted by him
to: laws have given him the power to do
keys: my name inscribed in the public register
Thrasyllus the son of Apollodorus
after he had adopted me in this manner
what_it_shows: The speaker, a sister's son whom Apollodorus adopted in his lifetime, says that after the adoption he was entered on the public register under the name 'Thrasyllus son of Apollodorus'. Entry followed a vote and an oath by the members of his genos and phratry.
context: A litigant's speech in an Athenian inheritance case (Isaeus 7, On the Estate of Apollodorus). Section 16 gives the general rule: the adopter swears over the sacrifice that the child is of an Athenian mother and rightly born, the members then vote, and only then is the child entered on the register. Section 17 is the speaker's own account of his case.
limits: (1) This is the speaker's own claim in a disputed case: section 28 says the opponents declared that Apollodorus 'had not adopted' him, so the entry is contested, not an agreed fact. (2) Section 16 (English): the child introduced, 'whether his own or an adopted son, is the offspring of an Athenian mother and born in wedlock', so adoption did not admit any outsider; the members must also vote before registration. (3) Section 1: the speaker says adoptions made by the adopter in his lifetime 'could not be disputed', which implies that other kinds (such as testamentary ones) could be. (4) The text does not say what phyle (tribe) the adoptee belonged to after adoption; 'fellow-tribesmen' appears only in section 36 about a gymnasiarchy. (5) Forster renders genos/phratry as 'families' and deme as 'ward'.
stance: reporting (a litigant's own speech, reported as his account)

quote_orig: Illud proprium est eius adoptionis, quae per populum fit, quod is, qui liberos in potestate habet, si se adrogandum dederit, non solum ipse potestati adrogatoris subicitur, sed etiam liberi eius in eiusdem fiunt potestate tanquam nepotes.
quote_en: It is peculiar to adoption by the vote of the people that children in the power of the person adrogated, as well as their father, fall under the power of the adrogator, assuming the position of grandchildren.
licence_note: Poste (Oxford 1904) translation as on the Grenoble page; the page gives no licence statement.
from_: It is peculiar to adoption by the vote
keys: assuming the position of grandchildren
fall under the power of the adrogator
children in the power of the person adrogated
what_it_shows: In adrogation (adoption by a vote of the people) the adoptee's own children pass into the adrogator's power as his grandchildren. The source gives this as a legal consequence of the adoption, not a blood relation.
context: Gaius 1.97-101 introduces adoption: adoptees are in the adopter's power; there are two forms (by the people, adrogatio, or by a magistrate's command); adrogation takes place only at Rome. 1.107 is the last point of that section; 1.108 begins the discussion of manus (marriage with hand).
limits: (1) Gaius speaks of potestas (power), not of name, tribe or inheritance, in this passage. (2) 1.107 applies to adrogation only, and Gaius marks it as 'peculiar' to that form. (3) 1.100: adrogation was done only at Rome; 1.101 and 1.104: women could not be adrogated or adopt. (4) 1.134 (Poste): 'A father is also divested of power over his children by giving them in adoption' (Latin: 'Praeterea parentes etiam liberos in adoptionem datos in potestate habere desinunt'), so a child given in adoption leaves the natural father's power. (5) 1.105: an adoptee could be given on to another adoptive father.

quote_orig: Illud proprium est illius adoptionis quae per sacrum oraculum fit, quod is qui liberos in potestate habet, si se adrogandum dederit, non solum ipse potestati adrogatoris subicitur, sed etiam liberi eius in eiusdem fiunt potestate tamquam nepotes. sic enim et divus Augustus non ante Tiberium adoptavit, quam is Germanicum adoptavit: ut protinus adoptione facta incipiat Germanicus Augusti nepos esse.
quote_en: It is peculiar to adoption by imperial rescript, that children in the power of the person adrogated, as well as their father, fall under the power of the adrogator, assuming the position of grandchildren. Thus Augustus did not adopt Tiberius until Tiberius had adopted Germanicus, in order that the latter might become his own grandson directly the second adoption was made.
licence_note: Moyle 1913 (Gutenberg #5983). Gutenberg licence statement appears in the file header (quoted under W-JUST-INST).
from_: It is peculiar to adoption by
to: directly the second adoption was made
keys: Thus Augustus did not adopt Tiberius
might become his own grandson
assuming the position of grandchildren
what_it_shows: Justinian's Institutes say that Augustus adopted Tiberius only after Tiberius had adopted Germanicus, so that Germanicus became Augustus' grandson at once. The text treats the adopted man's own children as grandchildren in the adoptive line.
context: Title XI 'De adoptionibus' of Justinian's Institutes (533), in the law of persons. 1.11.11 explains the consequence of adrogation for the adoptee's children; 1.11.12 then discusses adoption of a slave by his master.
limits: (1) 1.11.2 (same title, Moyle): under the law 'as now settled by our constitution', when a child in power is given in adoption to a stranger by his natural father, 'the power of the latter is not extinguished; no right passes to the adoptive father, nor is the person adopted in his power, though we have given a right of succession in case of the adoptive father dying intestate.' So Justinian's law did not make a stranger-adoptee the adopter's child in power; Gaius 1.134 states the older rule that such a child left the natural father's power. (2) 1.11.8: an adoptive child is 'in most respects' in the same position as a natural child. (3) 1.11.10: women cannot adopt (except by imperial indulgence). (4) The passage says nothing about name or tribe.

ref: Justinian, Institutes 3.2.2 (Moyle Title II, para. 2; 'Of the statutory succession of agnates')
quote_orig: Per adoptionem quoque adgnationis ius consistit, veluti inter filios naturales et eos quos pater eorum adoptavit (nec dubium est, quin proprie consanguinei appellentur): item si quis ex ceteris adgnatis tuis, veluti frater aut patruus aut denique is qui longiore gradu est, aliquem adoptaverit, adgnatio inter vos esse non dubitatur.
quote_en: The relation of agnation can also be established by adoption, for instance, between a man's own sons and those whom he has adopted, all of whom are properly called consanguinei in relation to one another. So, too, if your brother, or your paternal uncle, or even a more remote agnate, adopts any one, that person undoubtedly becomes one of your agnates.
from_: The relation of agnation can also be
to: undoubtedly becomes one of your agnates
keys: relation of agnation can also be established by adoption
properly called consanguinei
undoubtedly becomes one of your agnates
what_it_shows: Justinian's Institutes say that agnation (legal kinship through male links, which governs intestate succession) can be created by adoption. Adopted sons are called consanguinei of their adoptive brothers, and an adopted man becomes an agnate of the adopter's own agnates.
context: Book III, Title II of the Institutes ('Of the statutory succession of agnates'). Title I just before it (3.1.10-14) discusses the succession rights of adopted and emancipated children.
limits: (1) Inst. 3.1.11 (Moyle): 'Adoptive are thus not so well off as natural children in respect of rights of succession'; adoptive children emancipated 'are regarded as strangers ... because they lose the title and name of son or daughter, which they have acquired by a civil change, namely adoption'. (2) Inst. 3.1.14 (Moyle): on a will, the adopted son 'cannot obtain any part of the inheritance', because 'being related by no tie of blood, the adoptive father is not bound either to institute him heir or to disinherit him'. Justinian excepts adoption by a natural ascendant. (3) Inst. 1.11.2: the natural father's power is not extinguished by adoption of a child by a stranger. (4) Inst. 1.11.8 says adoptive children are 'in most respects' like natural children, not in all.

quote_orig: Velitis, iubeatis, uti L. Valerius L. Titio tam iure legeque filius siet, quam si ex eo patre matreque familias eius natus esset, utique ei vitae necisque in eum potestas siet, uti patri endo filio est. Haec ita, uti dixi, ita vos, Quirites, rogo.
quote_en: Express your desire and ordain that Lucius Valerius be the son of Lucius Titius as justly and lawfully as if he had been born of that father and the mother of his family, and that Titius have that power of life and death over Valerius which a father has over a son. This, just as I have stated it, I thus ask of you, fellow Romans.
licence_note: Rolfe (Loeb 1927) as on Perseids; licence status not verified (no licence line on the pages read).
from_: Express your desire and ordain that
to: I thus ask of you, fellow Romans
keys: as if he had been born of that father
be the son of Lucius Titius
the mother of his family
what_it_shows: The formula by which the people were asked to approve an adrogation makes the adoptee 'the son' of the adopter 'as justly and lawfully as if he had been born of that father and the mother of his family', and gives the adopter the father's power of life and death.
context: Gellius, Attic Nights 5.19, distinguishes adoptatio (before a magistrate, with a thrice-repeated sale) from adrogatio (before the comitia curiata, with pontifical oversight). Immediately before the formula he describes the oath and the procedure. The example names (L. Valerius, L. Titius) are given in the text; Gellius does not say that this was a real case.
limits: (1) Gellius 5.19.1-2 and 5.19.9: the formula is for adrogatio (the people's vote), not for adoptatio. (2) 5.19.10: no ward (pupillus) and no woman outside her father's power may be adrogated. (3) 5.19.11-12: Masurius Sabinus held that freedmen could be adopted by the freeborn, but said it was not permitted and should never be permitted for freedmen to 'usurp the privileges of the freeborn'. (4) 5.19.13: the same authority says an adoption of a slave by a praetor could be done under old law. (5) The legal fiction is of 'as if born', not a claim about blood or tribe.
stance: reporting (Gellius reporting older antiquarian sources; not his own view)

ref: Aulus Gellius, Noctes Atticae 5.19.15-16 (censor's speech quoted by Gellius)
quote_orig: In alia tribu patrem, in alia filium suffragium ferre, filium adoptivum tam procedere, quam si se natum habeat; absentis censeri iubere, ut ad censum nemini necessus sit venire.
quote_en: A father votes in one tribe, the son in another, an adopted son is of as much advantage as if one had a son of his own; orders are given to take the census of absentees, and hence it is not necessary for anyone to appear in person at the census.
licence_note: Rolfe (Loeb 1927) as on Perseids; licence status not verified.
from_: A father votes in one tribe, the
to: necessary for anyone to appear in person
keys: A father votes in one tribe
an adopted son is of as much advantage
as if one had a son of his own
what_it_shows: Gellius quotes a censor (named 'Publius Scipio') who listed among practices contrary to ancestral custom that an adoptive son was of advantage to his adoptive father 'as if one had a son of his own'. The same sentence says the father and the adopted son vote 'in one tribe' and 'in another' respectively. The text does not say which tribe the adoptee was enrolled in.
context: In 5.19.15 Gellius says he noticed that in a speech of Publius Scipio, delivered to the people as censor 'on morals', the speaker found fault with a number of practices contrary to the institutions of the ancestors, including adoptive sons counting for fathers' rewards. The quoted sentence is part of the speech.
limits: (1) This is a criticism of a practice, quoted by Gellius; it does not state the law on tribe. (2) The sentence can be read in more than one way: as a complaint that the adoptee and the adopter vote in different tribes, or as a description of a situation the speaker found objectionable. I did not find a commentary read that settles it (UNVERIFIED reading). (3) Gellius adds no comment on the tribe question. (4) The censor is cited only through Gellius's report.
stance: quoting opponent (a censor criticising adoption practice, reported by Gellius)

quote_orig: rogataque lex qua in familiam Claudiam et nomen Neronis transiret.
quote_en: It was noted by learned men, that no previous example of adoption into the patrician family of the Claudii was to be found; and that from Attus Clausus there had been one unbroken line. However, the emperor received formal thanks, and still more elaborate flattery was paid to Domitius. A law was passed, adopting him into the Claudian family with the name of Nero.
licence_note: Church and Brodribb translation as on MIT Classics Archive; licence not stated on the page read.
from_: It was noted by learned men
to: the Claudian family with the name of Nero
keys: adopting him into the Claudian family with the name of Nero
no previous example of adoption into the patrician family
one unbroken line
what_it_shows: Tacitus says a law (rogatio) adopted Domitius, later Nero, into the Claudian family 'with the name of Nero'. He adds that learned men knew of no earlier adoption into the patrician Claudii.
context: Annals 12.25-26: in the consulship of Caius Antistius and Marcus Suilius, Pallas pressed Claudius to adopt Domitius, Agrippina's son, over his own son Britannicus. Tacitus describes the adoption as political and as a court intrigue; the adoptee's transfer into the Claudian family and name is the legal point.
limits: (1) Tacitus presents the adoption as hastened by intrigue (Pallas, Agrippina) and says it was new for the patrician Claudii. (2) The passage does not describe the legal form beyond 'a law was passed' (rogata lex); other sources (Gellius 5.19; Justinian 1.11.11) show that the adrogation rogatio was the form for a citizen adoptee. (3) Tacitus says nothing about tribe or about the adoptee's sacra. (4) Tacitus wrote c. AD 115-117 about an event of about AD 50 (about 65 years earlier).

quote_orig: in ima cera Gaium Octauium etiam in familiam nomenque adoptauit;
quote_en: Other heirs [in remainder] were named at the close of the will, in which he also adopted Caius Octavius, who was to assume his name, into his family;
licence_note: Thomson/Reed 1883 (Gebbie) as on Perseids; no licence line read.
from_: in which he also adopted Caius Octavius
to: was to assume his name, into his family
keys: adopted Caius Octavius, who was to assume his name
into his family
in which he also adopted
what_it_shows: Suetonius says that in the will Caesar adopted Gaius Octavius 'into his family and name', i.e. the adoption was made by will. Octavian's later name 'Gaius Caesar' came from the great-uncle's will (Suetonius, Augustus 7).
context: Suetonius, Divus Iulius 83, on Caesar's last will (44 BC): Octavius was named heir for three-quarters of the estate and adopted in the last clause. Augustus 7 (Latin, read) says Octavian took the name 'Gai Caesaris' 'testamento maioris auunculi'.
limits: (1) Gaius 1.98 and Justinian 1.11.1 list only two forms of adoption (by the people, or by a magistrate's order); an adoption by will is not one of them, so this is an exceptional case. (My comparison of the texts; not stated by Suetonius.) (2) Suetonius reports the will; he does not describe the legal mechanism. (3) Suetonius Tib. 15 (Latin, read): after adoption the adoptee 'never more acted as master of a family' and his property became part of the father's peculium, so adoption did not give the adoptee independent property rights. (4) Suetonius says nothing about tribe or sacra here.

ref: Cicero, De domo sua 35 (speech to the pontifices, 57 BC)
quote_orig: quas adoptiones sicut alias innumerabilis hereditates nominis pecuniae sacrorum secutae sunt.
quote_en: And these adoptions, like others, more than I can count, were followed by the inheritance of the name and property and sacred rites of the family.
licence_note: Yonge translation as on Pomona page (no licence line).
from_: And these adoptions, like others, more
keys: followed by the inheritance of the name and property and sacred rites
these adoptions, like others
what_it_shows: Cicero says that adoptions of the kind he describes (of old men by young men, and of Aufidius and Pupius) were followed by the inheritance of name, property and sacred rites of the adopter's family. This is the speaker's own general statement, used in an argument against Clodius.
context: Cicero argues before the pontifices that Clodius' adoption into the plebeian Fonteii was invalid under pontifical law, to end Clodius' tribunate. He lists adoptions made for the sake of name, property and cult, and says Clodius lost his own family's sacra.
limits: (1) An advocate's argument in a hostile speech; Cicero's point is that Clodius' adoption was not a valid one. (2) The sentence says what followed adoptions 'like others', but gives no legal text. (3) Cicero also says Clodius was emancipated at once (section 37), which he presents as a sham; the same speech treats the adoptee as the adopter's son for the purpose of tribunate. (4) The speech says Clodius was not 'heir of his new father' (35), so the inheritance point is contested within the text.
stance: reporting (advocate's statement; Cicero is the speaker and is arguing against Clodius)

quote_orig: Gaio et Lucio intra triennium defunctis adoptatur ab Augusto simul cum fratre eorum M. Agrippa, coactus prius ipse Germanicum fratris sui filium adoptare. nec quicquam postea pro patre familias egit aut ius, quod amiserat, ex ulla parte retinuit.
quote_en: But Caius and Lucius being both carried off in the space of three years, he was adopted by Augustus, along with their brother Agrippa; being obliged in the first place to adopt Germanicus, his brother's son. After his adoption, he never more acted as master of a family, nor exercised, in the smallest degree, the rights which he had lost by it.
licence_note: Thomson/Reed 1883 (Gebbie) as on Perseids; no licence line read.
from_: But Caius and Lucius being both carried
to: the rights which he had lost by it
keys: he was adopted by Augustus
After his adoption, he never more acted as master of a family
the rights which he had lost by it
what_it_shows: Suetonius says Tiberius was adopted by Augustus (after being made to adopt Germanicus), which is a case of adoption into a dynastic family. He also says that after adoption Tiberius no longer acted as master of a household and lost his property rights, which are described as the father's peculium.
context: Suetonius, Tiberius 15: after the deaths of Gaius and Lucius Caesar, Augustus adopted Tiberius along with Agrippa; Tiberius had to adopt Germanicus first. The text then describes Tiberius' legal position under his adoptive father.
limits: (1) The passage is about political succession; Suetonius describes Tiberius' property situation as a restriction, which limits any claim that adoption made the adoptee's property his own. (2) Aug. 65 (Latin, read) says Tiberius was adopted 'in foro lege curiata', i.e. by the adrogation procedure. (3) The text says nothing about tribe.

quote_orig: ἐγυμνασιάρχουν ἐν τῷ δήμῳ καὶ ἐφιλοτιμήθην ὡς ὑὸς ὢν ἐκείνου, καὶ τὰς στρατείας, ὅσαι ἐγένοντο ἐν τῷ χρόνῳ τούτῳ, ἐστράτευμαι ἐν τῇ φυλῇ τῇ ἐκείνου καὶ ἐν τῷ δήμῳ
quote_en: But, in the circumstances, I consider it terrible and disgraceful that, when Menecles possessed property, I accepted adoption as his son and out of his property, before the land was sold, acted as gymnasiarch [note omitted] in his deme and won credit as his son, and served in his tribe and deme on all the campaigns which took place during that period;
licence_note: Forster (Loeb 1927) as on Perseids; a footnote on the gymnasiarch is omitted, marked. Greek from the same Perseids edition.
from_: served in his tribe and deme on all
to: which took place during that period
keys: served in his tribe and deme
won credit as his son
I accepted adoption as his son
what_it_shows: The adopted speaker says that as the son of Menecles he served on campaigns 'in his tribe and deme' (Greek: 'in the tribe of that man and in the deme'). In his own account the adoptee was in the adopter's phyle and deme, not only in the register.
context: Isaeus 2 is a speech by an adopted son defending the adoption made by Menecles, a childless man, against his uncle's claim. Section 42 is near the end, where the speaker says he has acted as Menecles' son in public life (gymnasiarchy in the deme, military service in the tribe).
limits: (1) This is the speaker's own claim in a contested case, not a neutral statement of law. (2) The text says 'his tribe' ('τῇ ἐκείνου', 'of that man'), which Forster reads as the adopter's tribe; the Greek phrase is short and I did not read a commentary on it (UNVERIFIED as to the legal rule). (3) Section 35 says the property the adoptee received was small (300 drachmae and a small house) while the uncle 'has a much larger share', so the adoptee's inheritance was not the whole estate. (4) The adoption itself was contested (sections 1, 19-26: the uncle alleges insanity or a woman's influence).

quote_orig: ποιησάμενος εἰσάγει με εἰς τοὺς φράτορας παρόντων τούτων, καὶ εἰς τοὺς δημότας με ἐγγράφει καὶ εἰς τοὺς ὀργεῶνας.
quote_en: The law thus allowing Menecles, because he was childless, to adopt a son, he adopted me, not by a will made at the point of death, as other citizens have done, nor during illness; but when he was sound in body and mind, and fully aware of what he was doing, he adopted me and introduced me to his fellow-wardsmen in the presence of my opponents and enrolled me among the demesmen and the members of his confraternity.
licence_note: Forster (Loeb 1927) as on Perseids; a footnote (on the 'confraternity', cf. Isaeus 9.30) is omitted.
from_: he adopted me, not by a will made
to: the demesmen and the members of his confraternity
keys: introduced me to his fellow-wardsmen
enrolled me among the demesmen
not by a will made at the point of death
what_it_shows: The speaker says a childless man adopted him in his lifetime, introduced him to the phratry (fellow-wardsmen), and enrolled him among the demesmen and in the orgeones (a religious association). He contrasts this with adoption by will made at death, which 'other citizens have done'.
context: Isaeus 2.13-14: the speaker first cites the law that lets a man with no legitimate sons adopt and dispose of his property; then describes his own adoption, which was in the adopter's lifetime and with registration before witnesses.
limits: (1) The speaker's own account in a contested case; the uncle says the adopter was not of sound mind (2.1, 2.19-26). (2) The text says adoption by will was used by other citizens: so testamentary adoption existed in Athens (contrast Isaeus 6.3-8, a will-adoption case). (3) Section 13 says the law permits adoption only for a man with no male issue. (4) 2.35: the adopted son received only a small share of the estate (see G-A7-11).

quote_orig: ὁ γὰρ νόμος οὐκ ἐᾷ ἐπανιέναι, ἐὰν μὴ ὑὸν καταλίπῃ γνήσιον.
quote_en: For the law does not allow the return of an adopted son to his original family, unless he leaves a legitimate son in the family which he quits.
licence_note: Forster (Loeb 1927) as on Perseids. An editorial note inside the sentence is omitted.
from_: the law does not allow the return
to: in the family which he quits
keys: the law does not allow the return of an adopted son to his original family
unless he leaves a legitimate son
what_it_shows: The speaker says the law does not let an adopted son return to his original family unless he leaves a legitimate son in the family he quits. Adoption, on this account, transfers the adoptee out of his birth family in law.
context: Isaeus 6 (estate of Philoctemon): Philoctemon, childless, adopted his sister's son Chaerestratus by will. An opponent (Androcles) claimed the adoptees were natural sons of Euctemon. Section 44 answers that the boys had been inscribed as adopted sons of the adopters and could not return.
limits: (1) A speaker's statement of law in an argument; it is not a quotation of the statute. (2) Section 44 has a condition: 'unless he leaves a legitimate son' (the return is allowed only if a son is left). (3) Section 5-6 and 8 describe a will-adoption; the speech's claim that the will was valid is itself disputed (Androcles alleged perjury). (4) The rule is about return; it does not by itself settle the name or tribe of the adoptee.

quote_orig: ὁμολογοῦμεν δʼ ἐναντίον ὑμῶν δεῖν τὰς ποιήσεις κυρίας εἶναι, ὅσαι ἂν κατὰ τοὺς νόμους δικαίως γένωνται.
own_translation_en: We admit before you that adoptions must be valid, all those that are made rightly according to the laws. (The speaker's side claims by descent, kata genos; the other side by adoption, kata poiesin. Team's own translation, not Murray's.)
licence_note: Murray's 1939 Loeb translation is NOT quoted (copyright not verified). Own translation by the researcher, labelled as such.
from_: We admit before you that adoptions
to: made rightly according to the laws
keys: ὁμολογοῦμεν δʼ ἐναντίον ὑμῶν
ὅσαι ἂν κατὰ τοὺς νόμους δικαίως γένωνται
what_it_shows: In this speech the speaker's side concedes that adoptions are valid when made rightly by the laws. The dispute is then between descent (kata genos) and adoption (kata poiesin) as the basis for the estate.
context: Demosthenes 44 (Against Leochares) concerns the estate of Archiades. The opponents claim by adoption; the speaker's side claims by blood descent (next of kin in the male line). Section 21-23 says Leocrates, adopted by Archiades, returned to his original family and left an adopted son in the house.
limits: (1) The concession is conditional: 'if rightly made in accordance with the laws'; the speaker argues the adoption in this case was not so made. (2) Section 12 (not quoted): the speaker says the law gives the inheritance to the nearest male kin when there are no children, which means that blood kin can outrank an adoptee in this case. (3) Section 21-23 show that an adopted son who left the adopter's house was challenged as against the laws (see Isaeus 6.44). (4) The text does not say what tribe the adoptee joined.

quote_orig: καὶ τῷ ἐμῷ παιδίῳ ἐθέμην τὸ ὄνομα τὸ ἐκείνου, ἵνα μὴ ἀνώνυμος ὁ οἶκος αὐτοῦ γένηται
quote_en: I, the adopted son, with the aid of my wife, the daughter of Philonides here, tended Menecles while he lived and gave his name to my little son, in order that his family might not lack a representative.
from_: I, the adopted son, with the aid
to: his family might not lack a representative
keys: gave his name to my little son
in order that his family might not lack a representative
what_it_shows: The adopted son says he gave the name of Menecles, his adoptive father, to his own little son, so that the house of Menecles would not be without a name. This is a custom of naming the next generation after the adopter; the text does not describe a legal rule.
context: Isaeus 2.36 is part of the speaker's account of the care he gave Menecles, his burial and the rites he performed for him, which he presents as the conduct of a true son.
limits: (1) It is a claim of custom and of conduct, not a rule of law. (2) The speaker's naming of his son is his own act, not a statement that the child inherited anything. (3) The text does not say whether the grandson had any legal claim on Menecles' estate.

quote_orig: Filios familias non solum natura, verum et adoptiones faciunt. Quod adoptionis nomen est quidem generale, in duas autem species dividitur, quarum altera adoptio similiter dicitur, altera adrogatio. adoptantur filii familias, adrogantur qui sui iuris sunt.
own_translation_en: Adoptions, as well as nature, make sons of families. The name adoption is general and divides into two kinds, one of which is called adoption and the other adrogation: sons of families are adopted, and those who are their own masters are adrogated. (Researcher's own translation, not a published one.)
licence_note: No published English quoted. Own translation, labelled.
from_: Filios familias non solum natura, verum
keys: Filios familias non solum natura
adoptiones faciunt
adrogantur qui sui iuris sunt
what_it_shows: The jurist Modestinus says that adoptions as well as nature make sons of families (filii familias); adoption of a son of a family and adrogation of a man sui iuris are the two kinds of adoption.
context: Digest 1.7 (De adoptionibus) opens with this definition. It is a short statement of the category, followed by the procedural rules in 1.7.2 (taken from Gaius 1 Inst., the same passage as Gaius 1.98-99).
limits: (1) A definition, not a rule about name, tribe or inheritance. (2) The title covers emancipation as well as adoption. (3) Dig. 1.7.10 (G-A7-17) limits the heir rights of an adopted grandson.

quote_orig: Si quis nepotem quasi ex filio natum quem in potestate habet consentiente filio adoptaverit, non adgnascitur avo suus heres, quippe cum post mortem avi quasi in patris sui reccidit potestatem.
own_translation_en: If someone adopts, with the son's consent, a grandson whom he has in his power, as if he were born of that son, the grandson does not become a suus heres of the grandfather, since after the grandfather's death he falls back into the power of his own father, as if. (Researcher's own translation, not a published one; the last clause is a literal rendering of 'quasi in patris sui reccidit potestatem'.)
from_: Si quis nepotem quasi ex filio natum
keys: non adgnascitur avo suus heres
quasi in patris sui reccidit potestatem
what_it_shows: Paulus says that a grandson adopted 'as if born of a son' (with the son's consent) does not become the grandfather's suus heres, because after the grandfather dies he falls back under his own father's power. The adoptee's place in the adopter's inheritance is therefore limited.
context: Digest 1.7.10 (Paulus) sits among rules on the adoption of grandsons (1.7.6-1.7.11), which explain when the consent of the son and the power relationships matter.
limits: (1) It is a restriction, not a grant of heirship. (2) It concerns the grandson's status as suus heres (family heir), not his name or tribe. (3) The grandfather's natural power and his son's consent are conditions in the case.
